key_insight: Temperature patterns from a vaginal wearable, combined with machine learning, may help distinguish people with PMOS/PCOS from those without it.
clinical_relevance: This could support earlier, more accessible screening for a common underdiagnosed endocrine condition using noninvasive data already captured across menstrual cycles.
method: 387 wearable temperature users completed a questionnaire and were classified as PMOS cases/controls when possible.
Three menstrual cycles per participant were sampled and converted into cycle-level and user-level temperature features, including ovulation-related temperature rise measures.
Logistic Regression, SVM, and Random Forest were tested with 5-fold nested cross-validation at both cycle and user levels.
evidence_signal: The study used 387 participants with an average age of 31.97 years, and the abstract reports moderate model discrimination when predicting PMOS from temperature-derived features.
watch_item: Self-reported PMOS status and a selected wearable-user sample may limit generalizability, so external validation in broader populations is needed.
paper_title: A digital health approach for identifying polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome using machine learning and body temperature
